questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Exciting and relevant electives for my academic interests, the nature around the city, a low language barrier, and the destination not being far away

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an intro week, however I missed it, because information about this and the courses arrived quite late, so I was not informed the semester would begin a month earlier than in my own country.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Since the host language is Norwegian, and my mother tongue is Danish, it was quite easy to navigate in the housing websites, but none were in English. This is a huge privilege compared to other exchange students, who do not speak a Scandinavian language. 

That being said, I was initially offered housing through my host institution, which I declined, because it was an 8 m2 room, including kitchen and bathroom, that was shared in bunk beds with another exchange students. From other exchange students who accepted this offer, I have only heard bad or medium things. 

Lastly, the housing opportunities can be a bit expensive in Bergen, and it’s difficult to find places, that are willing to rent short term (less than a year).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I was initially offered housing through my host institution, which I declined, because it was an 8 m2 room, including kitchen and bathroom, that was shared in bunk beds with another exchange student. From other exchange students who accepted this offer, I have only heard bad or medium things and accounts of no personal space. 

Lastly, the housing opportunities can be a bit expensive in Bergen, and it’s difficult to find places, that are willing to rent short term (less than a year).

questions.answer: It was easy to get an overview of courses available to exchange students in English.  However not easy to find which courses in Norwegian you can apply for before the deadline for ola.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was a long list of courses and generally good communication with the host institution over outlook. The university website also had boxes to check off and pages with reminders to do as an exchange student.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the classes I applied for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Find out more about what courses you are able to apply for in Norwegian as well, if you believe you are able to follow along.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took a theoretical course in digital culture at humanities and a methodological course on computational text analysis in linguistics. In Copenhagen, I study a master in social data science. 

Both were master level at 15 ects points.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching varied a lot between the two courses I took in Bergen. 

The theoretical course was much more active and discussion-based than that of UCPH, and more comparable to seminars in form. We also had to hand in weekly essays discussing self chosen topics with the reading of the week. I found it was a very good course form for following and learning the syllabus throughout the semester.

For the course in computational linguistics, I was more disappointed with the teaching style, as it was much less involved, even though we had to code in R, which several students did not have experience in (it was not required). From UCPH, I have had good experience with learning a method and a programming language simultaneously, where we e.g. were given weekly coding challenges, which in my opinion works very well. 

Both courses had very little attendance. I had preferred a bit more classes a week.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
DIKULT302 25H / Key Theories of Digital Culture

It was a great course for discussing and thinking about how to use theory in practice, especially if you (as I did) wanted to also brainstorm about your master thesis topic.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Generally Norway is not that much more expensive than Denmark, with exceptions of specific items such as alcohol or cheese (and for some reason cucumber). But the Norwegian krone was also quite low during my exchange, which was an advantage as a Dane. 

The housing is expensive, and the transport is not cheap either. Not many people bike, as the city is very hilly, so you will have to get accustomed to walking and taking public transport. 

If you want to go on nature trips around Bergen and Norway in general, this can also quickly become expensive with the trains. However, it is possible to make it cheaper, and the city’s public transport by bus covers a very large area.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Alcohol was expensive, but that was expected. Remember to ask for student discount everywhere, it is widely used in Bergen. 

The supermarket prices were less expensive than I thought.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There are many activities available for students in Bergen, both as a part of UIB and outside of it. 
There are often concerts and art exhibitions, very cool events and cute cafes! I also volunteered at a concert place called Hulen, which I would really recommend if you like live music and want to practice your Norwegian. 

Athletically, there are also many sports and outdoor associations, so keep a look out for that. I became a member in one of the student gyms, which also gave access to a swimming pool, I would also recommend that. I heard a lot of people found places to climb as well. 

There are also student cafes and bars, I spent time at Ad Fontes, where there is free coffee, tea, and water of course.

Overall, a very active student city.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Engage in some of the student associations there are, people are quite welcoming. Maybe become a volunteer at one of the student bars or sports clubs.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go for hikes in the nearby mountains, you can see very beautiful nature on a short amount of time. There are apps such as UT, where you can see the difficulty levels of the routes. 

Also try to plan weekend trips in good time and get in touch with other exchange students and Norwegians. There are cabins to rent through DNT.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, quite similar to danish culture. The language is a bit more tricky, because of the dialect, but it’s possible!!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Engage in student associations.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: As I did not live in housing afforded by the host institution, I found it challenging to meet new people. I heard many of the other exchange students met each other there.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The great connection to nature and the language is amazing

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Try to find space in your calendar to join weekend trips to the mountains, even if you do not have much experience with hiking. And take initiative.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Go to the cold plunge and sauna.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Finding out what I wanted to write my master thesis on, creating a stable weekly routine, and experiencing beautiful hikes.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Meeting people when you don’t live in student housing.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
